prompt: A 100 GB gp3 volume holds 3 GB of files. What does the month bill for?
hint: A volume is a block device.

choices.text: The 3 GB of files it holds
choices.why: That is how an S3 bucket is billed, by what it stores. A volume is billed by its size.

choices.text: The 100 GB that were provisioned
choices.why: Right. A gp3 volume costs the same full or empty: 100 × 0.1520 = 15.20 a month.

choices.text: The reads and writes made to it during the month
choices.why: Requests are billed on S3 and Lambda. The gp3 line on the sheet is per GB-month.

choices.text: Nothing, while no instance is running
choices.why: A stopped instance stops its hours; the disk still exists and keeps its GB-months.

prompt: Match each unit to a service billed in it.
hint: Lessons 4, 5, 6 and 8.

prompt: An instance is stopped for the weekend. Which of its lines keeps growing?
hint: What still exists while it is stopped?

choices.text: Its instance-hours, at a reduced rate
choices.why: A stopped instance stops its instance-hours entirely; there is no reduced rate on the sheet.

choices.text: None: stopping it stops every charge
choices.why: Stopping ends the machine's hours, not the disk's existence.

choices.text: The GB-months of its volume
choices.why: Right. The volume is billed for existing, whether a machine is using it or not.

choices.text: Its traffic out to the internet
choices.why: Traffic is billed for use, and a stopped machine sends nothing.

prompt: Which of these are billed for existing, even when nothing happens? Choose all that apply.
hint: Hours and provisioned gigabytes accrue on their own.

choices.text: An hour of a NAT gateway
choices.why: Yes: 0.0930 an hour, carrying traffic or not.

choices.text: A Lambda request
choices.why: Billed for use: a function nobody calls costs nothing.

choices.text: An hour of a public IPv4 address
choices.why: Yes: 0.0050 an hour, in use or idle.

choices.text: A gigabyte sent to the internet
choices.why: Billed for use: no traffic, no charge.

choices.text: A GB-month of a provisioned gp3 volume
choices.why: Yes: the size you asked for, full or empty.

prompt: Why does prices.py name one version of each offer instead of asking for the latest?
hint: What happens to a price over a year?

choices.text: Older versions are cheaper to download
choices.why: Downloading the list costs nothing; the reason is what the numbers mean over time.

choices.text: The latest version is not public until the month closes
choices.why: Every version is public as soon as it is published, the current one included.

choices.text: So the sheet prints the same numbers every time it runs
choices.why: Right. A pinned version makes each number in the lessons reproducible.

choices.text: A pinned version is the price a company actually pays
choices.why: The list is the public price before tax, discounts, credits and commitments.

prompt: Put the steps of reading one price out of an offer file in order.
hint: Meter first, money last.
items: Select the product by its usagetype
Read pricePerUnit in its price dimension
trap: The term is looked up by SKU, so the product has to be found first.

prompt: In the usage type SAE1-Request, what does SAE1 say?
hint: The file was sa-east-1's.

choices.text: The version of the offer
choices.why: The version is a timestamp, 20260919002359 for Lambda.

choices.text: Only the region, São Paulo
choices.why: Right. The prefix names the region; Request names what is counted.

choices.text: The first price tier
choices.why: Tiers are ranges inside a price dimension, beginRange and endRange.

choices.text: The SKU of the product
choices.why: The SKU was a separate opaque code, 7TZ969MZND3Z6HD7.

prompt: In a price list product, the attribute that says what is being measured is called ___
hint: SAE1-Request is one of its values.

prompt: A NAT gateway in sa-east-1 is 0.0930 USD an hour. What do its hours cost in a 730-hour month?
hint: Price times hours.

prompt: Why does the estimate use a month of 730 hours?
hint: Divide a year.

choices.text: It is the length of a 30-day month
choices.why: Thirty days are 720 hours; 730 is an average, not a real month.

choices.text: All 8,760 hours of a year, split into twelve equal months
choices.why: Right, the calculators' convention, so every month costs the same.

choices.text: AWS bills 730 hours whatever the calendar says
choices.why: The bill counts the hours that ran; 730 is a convention for estimating.

choices.text: It leaves ten hours a month for maintenance
choices.why: Nothing is set aside; it is simply a year's hours in twelve equal parts.

prompt: A colleague's estimate lists the load balancer at 0.0340 an hour and nothing else for it. What is missing?
hint: Is the hour the only way it is billed?

choices.text: A second charge for all the load it handles
choices.why: Right. The capacity units are billed on top of the hour and are not on the sheet.

choices.text: Its GB-months of storage
choices.why: A load balancer stores nothing to bill by the GB-month.

choices.text: A price per Lambda request it forwards
choices.why: Lambda requests are billed by Lambda, and this design has no function.

choices.text: Nothing, the hour covers everything
choices.why: The estimate says the opposite: the hour is only the part that is on the sheet.

prompt: The same two t3.medium machines in us-east-1, at 0.04160 an hour: what do they cost in a 730-hour month?
hint: Two machines, one price, 730 hours.

prompt: A public IPv4 address costs 0.0050 USD an hour, in use or idle. What does one address cost in a year of 8,760 hours?
hint: Price times the hours of a year.

prompt: Machines in private subnets read 200 GB from S3 through a NAT gateway. What does that traffic add?
hint: The gateway is billed twice.

choices.text: Nothing, traffic inside a region is always free
choices.why: The NAT gateway charges for every gigabyte it processes, wherever it goes.

choices.text: 0.1500 per GB, as traffic out to the internet
choices.why: The bytes never leave for the internet; the charge is the gateway's processing.

choices.text: Only the gateway's hourly price
choices.why: The hours are billed whether or not traffic passes; processing is a second line.

choices.text: 18.60 USD of processing, at 0.0930 per GB
choices.why: Right, and a gateway endpoint for S3 would carry the same reads for nothing.

prompt: A team adds a read replica in a second zone and says it costs "only the machine". Which line did they miss?
hint: What has to reach the replica, and from where?

choices.text: A second NAT gateway for the replica
choices.why: A replica receives changes from the primary inside the network; it needs no NAT.

choices.text: Every GB crossing between zones
choices.why: Right: 0.0100 leaving one zone and 0.0100 entering the other, 0.02 for each gigabyte of changes.

choices.text: Data out to the internet for every change
choices.why: The changes stay inside the provider; the internet price does not apply.

choices.text: A fee for keeping a second zone open
choices.why: Zones have no fee of their own; what costs is the traffic between them.

prompt: Match each surprise line to the change that removes it.
hint: One fix per line.

pairs.left: S3 reads through the NAT gateway
a volume left by a deleted instance

prompt: A backup job copies 1,000 GB a month from one zone to another. At 0.0100 per GB in each direction, what does the crossing cost a month?
hint: Both sides of the crossing are billed.

prompt: A Lambda function stuck in a loop passes the free million requests on day 3. What happens next?
hint: Is a free tier a limit on spending?

choices.text: The function is stopped until next month
choices.why: Nothing stops it; that is what "a free tier is not a cap" means.

choices.text: AWS sends a warning and waits for approval
choices.why: No approval is asked for. A warning only exists if somebody set up a budget.

choices.text: It keeps running and keeps billing
choices.why: Right: 0.20 per million requests past the allowance, and the GB-second price, for as long as the loop runs.

choices.text: The requests fail with an error
choices.why: Past the allowance the next price dimension applies; requests keep working.

prompt: A function with 512 MB runs 200 ms per request, 10 million requests in a month. With the free allowance, what does the month cost?
hint: Requests past 1 million, plus GB-seconds past 400,000.

prompt: A company runs twenty small functions in three regions, each well under a million requests a month. Why is the bill not zero?
hint: Whose is the allowance?

choices.text: Each region has its own smaller allowance
choices.why: The usage type is Global-Request: one allowance, not one per region.

choices.text: One allowance covers the whole account
choices.why: Right. Twenty functions together pass the one million the account has.

choices.text: Only the first function created is free
choices.why: The allowance counts requests and GB-seconds, not functions.

choices.text: Free tiers do not apply outside us-east-1
choices.why: The sheet prints the same allowance in both columns.

prompt: A machine was free for the first twelve months of an account. What happens in month thirteen if nobody acts?
hint: What does the end of a trial end?

choices.text: It is deleted with its data
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; the discount ends and the machine carries on.

choices.text: It is stopped until somebody pays the invoice
choices.why: That is the credit trials of Google Cloud and Azure, not an allowance on a paid account.

choices.text: It keeps running, and every hour is billed at full price
choices.why: Right. Nobody is told; the next bill is the message.

choices.text: It moves to a smaller size that is still free
choices.why: Providers do not resize your machines; it stays as it was, now billed.

prompt: t3.medium in sa-east-1: 0.06720 an hour on demand, 0.03860 reserved for a year. What is the discount, in percent, to one decimal?
hint: One minus the ratio, times 100.

prompt: What does "no upfront" mean on a 1-year reservation?
hint: Is there a promise?

choices.text: Every hour of the year is paid, used or not
choices.why: Right. For a t3.medium that is 0.03860 × 8,760 = 338.14 owed.

choices.text: You pay only for the hours the machine runs
choices.why: That is on demand. A reservation bills every hour of the term.

choices.text: You may cancel whenever you like, at no cost
choices.why: The promise is the price of the discount; the remaining months stay billed.

choices.text: The discount starts only in the second year
choices.why: The reserved price applies from the first hour; there is no second year in a 1-year term.

prompt: A test environment on a t3.medium runs weekdays from 9 to 18, about 27% of the hours. Reserved at 0.03860 or on demand at 0.06720?
hint: Compare with the break-even share of hours.

choices.text: Reserved: the discount is 42.6%
choices.why: The discount only pays if the machine runs over 57.4% of the hours.

choices.text: Reserved, and stop it at night to save more
choices.why: A reservation bills the night hours whether the machine is stopped or not.

choices.text: Either: they cost the same over a year
choices.why: They cost the same only at 57.4% of the hours; 27% is far below.

choices.text: On demand, well under break-even
choices.why: Right: it runs far below 57.4% of the hours; 27% at 0.06720 is about 0.018 per hour of the year, against 0.03860 reserved.

prompt: An application runs 2 machines every hour and up to 6 at its busiest. How many should be reserved?
hint: Which machines are used every hour?

choices.text: 6, to cover the peak
choices.why: Four of the six would be paid for every hour and used on a few days.

choices.text: 4, the average
choices.why: Two of those four would sit idle for much of the year, still billed.

choices.text: 2, the floor that always runs
choices.why: Right. Those two run every hour, so every hour of the promise is used.

choices.text: None: reservations never pay off
choices.why: At 42.6% off, a machine running every hour saves 20.88 a month.

prompt: Commit to the ___ of your usage, not to the peak.
hint: The machines that run every hour.

prompt: Why is there no spot price on the course's sheet?
hint: What moves a spot price?

choices.text: Spot capacity is free
choices.why: It is sold at a discount, not given away.

choices.text: It never stays fixed: it moves with supply and demand
choices.why: Right. It is published as a price history, not in the offer files.

choices.text: Only reserved customers may buy it
choices.why: Any account can ask for spot capacity; the price is the issue.

choices.text: prices.py was written before spot existed
choices.why: The sheet leaves it out on purpose: a fixed number would be wrong before you read it.

prompt: Which of these belongs on a spot machine?
hint: What survives the notice?

choices.text: The only database of a shop
choices.why: The only copy of anything is what a reclaimed machine takes with it.

choices.text: A ten-hour job that saves nothing until it ends
choices.why: Two minutes' notice at hour nine loses nine hours of work.

choices.text: Workers taking video conversions from a queue
choices.why: Right. An unfinished conversion goes back on the queue and another worker does it.

choices.text: The single instance that serves the whole website
choices.why: When it is reclaimed, the site is down until a new one starts.

prompt: A team wants to cut its compute bill with spot. Which of these designs make that safe? Choose all that apply.
hint: The work must survive, not the machine.

choices.text: Tasks that record their progress as they go
choices.why: Yes: a reclaimed machine loses one piece, not the job.

choices.text: An on-demand floor with spot machines above it
choices.why: Yes: if every spot machine goes, the service is slower, not down.

choices.text: Moving the primary database to spot to save the most
choices.why: The only copy of anything does not belong on capacity that is taken back.

choices.text: Tasks that are safe to do twice
choices.why: Yes: a task interrupted halfway is simply done again.

choices.text: A reservation for the spot machines
choices.why: Spot and reservations are different offers; a reservation is a promise to pay, not a guard against reclaiming.

prompt: A budget alert tells you about the spending; it does not ___ anything.
hint: What does spending do after the message?

prompt: A process runs away on day 12 of a month with a 400 USD budget. Put the alerts in the order they fire.
hint: The projection sees the trend before the spending reaches it.
trap: The forecast is the first, not the last: it projects the month from the spending so far.

prompt: Why set thresholds at 50% and 80%, and not only at 100%?
hint: How old are the numbers a budget compares?

choices.text: Providers charge less for alerts below 100%
choices.why: The price of an alert is not the reason; timing is.

choices.text: A 100% alert arrives after the money is spent
choices.why: Right. Billing data is hours behind, so the early thresholds are the ones you can act on.

choices.text: The API refuses a budget with one threshold
choices.why: One notification is a valid budget; it is just a late one.

choices.text: At 100% the account is blocked, so no alert is sent
choices.why: Nothing is blocked at 100%; spending carries on past the limit.

prompt: The budget file passed the CLI's check and failed with NoCredentials. What does that prove about the budget?
hint: What did the CLI do before looking for credentials?

choices.text: It was created and is waiting for approval
choices.why: Nothing reached AWS: the call stopped on this laptop, for want of credentials.

choices.text: Its limit of 400 is a sensible one
choices.why: The check reads field names and types; it has no opinion on the amount.

choices.text: It will send its e-mails once an account exists
choices.why: The check says the shape is right, not that the subscriber will receive anything.

choices.text: Its fields match the operation's definition
choices.why: Right, and only that: the misspelt copy failed the same check with ParamValidation.

prompt: Every resource carries team=payments, yet Cost Explorer cannot group by team. What is the likely cause?
hint: A tag on a resource and a tag in the bill are two steps.

choices.text: Tags only work in us-east-1
choices.why: Tags work in every region; the missing step is in billing.

choices.text: The key should have been written Team
choices.why: Case matters for consistency, but any spelling can be activated.

choices.text: It was never activated as a cost allocation tag
choices.why: Right. Until it is activated, the resources carry it and the reports ignore it.

choices.text: Cost Explorer groups by service only
choices.why: It groups by service, region, tag and day.

prompt: Google Cloud calls its key and value pairs on resources ___
hint: Not tags.

prompt: Match each tag key to the question it answers.
hint: Three keys, three questions.

pairs.right: Whom do we ask about it?
Which product is it spent on?
Can it be switched off at night?

prompt: The bill went from 298.64 to 900 in a year. Which number says whether that is healthy?
hint: Divide by what the business sells.

choices.text: The yearly total
choices.why: The total tripled; alone, it cannot say whether that is growth or waste.

choices.text: The share of the bill spent on machines
choices.why: A share says where money goes, not whether the growth paid for itself.

choices.text: The number of services on the bill
choices.why: More services says nothing about cost against the work done.

choices.text: The cost per active user
choices.why: Right: 0.15 then 0.075, so each user became cheaper to serve.

prompt: A data pipeline's cost per gigabyte processed has risen every month for a year while volume grew. What does it point to?
hint: Healthy growth makes each unit cheaper or keeps it flat.

choices.text: Something in it grows faster than the data
choices.why: Right: something like storage never deleted or a query scanning all history each run.

choices.text: The pipeline is succeeding: more data, more cost
choices.why: More data explains a rising total, not a rising cost per gigabyte.

choices.text: Prices on the list went up
choices.why: A price rise would show in the offer versions, and it would raise every customer's unit cost at once; a year of steady rises points at the design.

choices.text: The unit was chosen badly and should be changed
choices.why: Changing the unit hides the trend; the number is doing its job by showing it.

prompt: Match each provider's billing export to where it is delivered.
hint: A bucket, a warehouse and a storage account.

prompt: A function costs about 1.03 USD per million requests; a t3.medium costs 49.06 a month. An API gets 5 million requests a month. Which is cheaper?
hint: Where is the crossover?

choices.text: The machine, because it is always on
choices.why: Always on is what makes it cost 49.06 whatever it serves.

choices.text: They cost the same at any volume of traffic
choices.why: They are equal only near 47 million requests a month.

choices.text: The function: about 5.17 against 49.06
choices.why: Right. Five million is far below the 47 million where the two meet.

choices.text: The reserved machine
choices.why: Reserved it is 28.18 a month, still more than five times the function.

prompt: Moving the estimate to us-east-1 cuts most lines. What does the move cost instead?
hint: Lesson 9.

choices.text: Nothing: the same services, cheaper
choices.why: Every saving in the table is bought with something else, and this one with distance.

choices.text: Distance and latency to its users
choices.why: Right. Virginia is a long round trip from São Paulo.

choices.text: A higher price for public IPv4 addresses
choices.why: The sheet prints 0.0050 an hour in both regions.

choices.text: A second NAT gateway in each region
choices.why: The design moves; it does not double.

prompt: Order these from cheapest to dearest per GB-month in sa-east-1.
hint: Cold object storage at one end, a shared file system at the other.
trap: gp3 above S3 Standard is the one people swap: 0.1520 against 0.04050.

prompt: A team deleted its last instance, yet next month's bill still has a small line counted in hours. Which is the likeliest?
hint: Which unit is billed for existing, by the hour, with no machine?

choices.text: Data transfer in from the internet
choices.why: Traffic in is 0.0000 on the sheet, and it is counted in GB, not hours.

choices.text: The deleted instance, billed while stopped
choices.why: A deleted instance has no hours; stopping or deleting ends them.

choices.text: An Elastic IP address still allocated
choices.why: Right: an idle address is 0.0050 an hour, 3.65 a month, until somebody releases it.

choices.text: A budget, which is charged per alert
choices.why: Nothing on the sheet prices a budget; the line comes from something left behind.

prompt: Which pair of tools answers "who spent it" and "is our growth healthy"?
hint: One is attached to resources; one is a division.

choices.text: Budgets and spot capacity
choices.why: A budget warns about a total; spot is a way to pay less.

choices.text: Reservations and free allowances
choices.why: Both are discounts; neither says who spent or whether it was worth it.

choices.text: The price list and the 730-hour month
choices.why: Those build an estimate; they say nothing about the bill that arrived.

choices.text: Tags on each resource, and unit cost
choices.why: Right: tags attribute each line to a team, and unit cost divides the total by what the business sells.
